name: Dark Olive-Buff
lede: Dark Olive-Buff darkens [[olive-buff]], a muted yellow-brown Ridgway plotted in 1912, and it is one of the most common colors in our painting archive, present in about one painting in eight.

sections.title: A Ridgway hue, darkened
sections.body:
The name applies dark to [[olive-buff]], which Robert Ridgway placed on plate XL of his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*, hue 21′′′ [1]. Buff names a pale yellowish tan, after the color of buffalo hide leather, and olive shifts it toward green-grey [1]. The ISCC-NBS *Dictionary of Color Names* later filed this darkened form in 1955 as block 91 [1].

Its closest measured neighbor is [[ecru-olive]], only 3.0 units away and almost the same color; [[dust]] is a little duller and [[dust]] darker [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a common match in our archive: 2,924 of 23,781 paintings, 12.3 per cent, carry it, almost always as a highlight rather than a shadow (83 per cent of its appearances) [3]. It is especially frequent in Kalighat paintings, 43 of 96, 3.6 times the archive's overall rate, and in works by the Dutch portraitist Jan Maurits Quinkhard, 19 of his 40 paintings [3]. The earliest dated match is a Roman-period Egyptian funerary portrait from around the year 25, a floor on the color's age in painting rather than a claim of its first appearance [3]. As photographed: these are computed color matches on museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not a pigment test [3].
